title: Why Do Cats Lick Each Other? It's Not Always Friendship!
summary: Have you ever seen one cat licking another cat's head and thought, "Aww, best friends!"? Scientists say: not so fast. That licking has a fancy name — allogrooming. It means one animal grooms another. And it turns out cats do it for lots of reasons. Some are sweet. Some are sneaky. In a 1998 study, scientists watched 25 cats living together. They were surprised to find fighting or grumpy behavior in about 35 out of 100 licking sessions. That's a lot! So licking isn't always about love. Sometimes it's a way to say, "Hey, let's not fight." It's like a peace offering. A newer study led by Morgane Van Belle at Ghent University in Belgium watched videos of 53 homes with two cats. The team saw cats licking each other while cuddling and copying each other's poses. That probably helps them bond. But they also saw licking turn into wrestling — grabbing with front paws and tumbling around. So licking can be a signal that says, "Playtime?" And sometimes it's followed by stress signs, like lip licking or ear twitching. That's when licking might mean, "Please calm down, I don't want a fight." Most licking targets the ears. Why? The skin there is packed with nerve endings, so it feels relaxing. Horses and monkeys relax when groomed, too. Scientists still don't know everything. As cat expert Dr. Terry Curtis says: "Congratulations, you got a cat. Let the mystery begin."
why_it_matters: If you have a cat at home, watching how it licks or gets licked can help you tell when it wants to play and when it needs quiet space.

background_read: Cats often live in groups called colonies, especially where people leave food out, so they need ways to get along with each other.
Many animals groom each other: monkeys pick through each other's fur, and horses stand still and relax when another horse nibbles their back.

Scientists called ethologists study how animals behave. Ghent University (a university in Belgium) is one place where researchers watch videos of cats to figure out what cats are saying to each other.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists who study cats, including Morgane Van Belle at Ghent University in Belgium, and cat expert Dr. Terry Curtis.
WHAT: Studies show that when cats lick each other (allogrooming), it can mean bonding, an invitation to play, or a way to stop a fight.
WHERE: In a group of 25 cats living together in a 1998 study, and in 53 homes with two cats in a newer video study.
WHY: Licking is not always a sign of friendship — about 35 out of 100 licking sessions came with fighting, so it can be a 'peace offering' that keeps the group calm.

perspectives.description: They see licking as a sweet sign that cats are close friends, and they like that grooming feels good — especially around the ears, where the skin has lots of nerve endings.
They warn that licking is more complicated than it looks: in the 1998 study, about 35 out of 100 licking sessions included grumpy or fighting behavior, so it is not always about love.
They may mistake every lick for friendship. Experts say you should also watch for stress signs like lip licking or ear twitching, which can mean 'please calm down'.
